The story relies almost entirely on exteriority—focusing heavily on observable actions, physical details of the setting, and brief, utilitarian dialogue. While there are very brief moments of interiority (such as Ilse remembering that she needs to buy glue and windshield cleaner, or recognizing the regulars' routines), the narrative deliberately withholds her deeper feelings and inner emotional life. Even at the end, when her phone rings, her internal reaction to "Jonas" is left completely unstated, conveyed purely through the external action of letting the screen go dark. Because it avoids introspection and maintains a single, muted, and stoic tone throughout, it does not portray a broad spectrum of emotions or achieve a balance between action and introspection as defined by emotional flexibility.
